2.102.m: Kuñjala said: / I shall tell you everything, my child, which you have now spoken to me, / regarding the sorrow of both of them, and from what it arose, O best of the twice-born.
Once the great goddess Pārvatī, foremost among women, / sporting, spoke this word to the great-souled Īśvara:
‘O Mahādeva, a great pregnancy-craving has arisen in my heart; / show me the forest, the best of forests, before my eyes.’
The glorious Mahādeva said: / ‘So be it, O Mahādevī! I shall show you the holy Nandana, / filled with gods and frequented by the twice-born and the Siddhas.’
Having thus addressed that goddess, eager to go to that Nandana grove itself / together with her and his gaṇas, the god [mounted]
the bull that goes everywhere, handsome, its divine back adorned with ornaments, / equipped with garlands of bells, wearing nets of tinkling bells,
adorned with chowries, silken cords, and strings of pearls, / resembling a swan and the moon, possessing charming auspicious marks.
Mounted upon it, Mahādeva was surrounded by ten million gaṇas: / Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, Mahākāla, Skanda, Caṇḍa, and the delightful ones,
Vīrabhadra, Gaṇeśa, Puṣpadanta, Maṇīśvara, / Atibala, Subala by name, Meghanāda, Ghaṭāvaha,
Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Kālida, Pulinda, Vīrabāhuka, / Keśarin, Kiṅkara by name, Caṇḍahāsa, Prajāpati.
These and many others, Sanaka and the rest, mighty in penance— / accompanied by tens of millions of gaṇas, Śiva was surrounded.
Reaching the Nandana grove, frequented by gods and kinnaras, / Mahādeva entered along with his gaṇas and the goddess.
The lord of gods showed the mountain's daughter the very beautiful [grove], / endowed with various trees and filled with many flowers,
abounding with divine plantain groves, and flowering campaka trees, / with lovely blooming mallikās, and dense with clusters of mālatī.
shining with excellent groves of pāṭala trees with ever-blossoming branches, / and with great sandal trees of charming fragrance;
frequented by groves of devadāru trees, filled with lofty trees, / with sarala pines and coconuts, and likewise with areca-nut palms;
filled with large trees accompanied by the wafting of fragrances, / with divine date and jackfruit trees bent low by the weight of their fruit;
adorned with saptaparṇa trees glowing like the radiance of fire, / and ever endowed with the beauty of blossoms through rājavṛkṣa and kadaṃba trees;
filled with large rose-apple and neem trees, with citron trees, / with oranges and sindhuvāras, with priyālas, śālas, and tindukas;
adorned with rose-apple trees, with uduṃbaras and kapitthas, / filled with lakucas having fragrant flowers and blossoming nāgas;
and with mango trees, foremost of fruits, dark like rain-clouds; / with divine groves of dark śāla trees, and thickets of creepers stretching around;
and frequented by large tamāla trees resembling the sun: / the auspicious Nandana grove, thus adorned, was shown by Śiva;
and adorned with all other trees resembling a dark forest, / endowed with all desired fruits and yielding auspicious rewards;
the Nandana forest was adorned with most sacred wish-granting trees, / and filled with the diverse cries of birds in sweet voices;
echoing with the sweet, auspicious songs of cuckoos, / and resounding with the calls of birds greedy for floral nectar;
crowded with various trees, filled with herds of diverse beasts; / and because of the various fragrant blossoms fallen from the trees onto the ground,
that earth shines, O son, as though worshipped with fragrant flowers. / There are most sacred ponds there, clear with the fragrance of lotuses,
filled with waters, O son, frequented by geese and kāraṇḍava ducks, / with lakes resembling oceans, revered for their fragrant waters.
The great Nandana shines everywhere with hosts of apsarases, / with aerial chariots, white finials, and splendid golden poles.
The Nandana, the king of forests, with palaces coated with stucco, / shines brightly here and there with great hosts of kinnaras,
with gandharvas and beautiful apsarases, O best of the twice-born, / with the pastimes of the gods, and with multitudes of sages who are excellent yogins.
Everywhere the sacred abode of Nandana shone.
Having thus beheld the auspicious Nandana—the abode of the meritorious, a mine of bliss endowed with the quality of tranquility—the noble and magnanimous Bhava together with the goddess,

where the wish-granting tree, endowed with the capacity to grant desires through blossoms and fruits, / its golden form shining with rays equaling the brilliance of hosts of suns, stood in the Nandana forest,
beholding such a king of trees, the goddess spoke to Śiva: / “Tell me the name of this, O Lord, the sacred [tree] among all sacred trees.”
Like the foremost sun among luminous bodies all around, Śiva spoke to the goddess: / Śiva said: “Great and auspicious is its renown; just as Madhusūdana is chief among the gods,
and the river of the gods is chief among rivers, and the Creator Dhātṛ is the maker of creation, / and just as the gentle moon is foremost among bringers of delight, and the earth among the elements,
and just as the king of mountains is chief among mountains, and the ocean among reservoirs of water, / and as grain is chief among healing herbs, O goddess, and the Himālaya among mountains,
and just as the science of the self is supreme among sciences, and a monarch among all people in the worlds, / even so is this king of trees foremost: a host to all, dear to the lord of the gods.”

Śrī Pārvatī said: “O Śambhu, recount to me the auspicious, most sacred virtues of this sovereign of trees.” / Hearing her speech, the god spoke all concerning the beneficial nature of that tree to the goddess:
“Whatever the most holy gods, godlike beings, and foremost deities imagine, O beloved, / that very thing this tree gives to them for their welfare; its name is the Kalpadruma, the highest [of trees].
And from it arise all meritorious things, difficult to attain here even by those rich in austerities; / the supreme gods enjoy its divine gems, dearer than life itself.”
The goddess heard the words of Śiva and wondered in her mind; / with his consent, she conceived in thought a jewel of a woman, virtuous and fair.

From that excellent tree the mountain-born goddess obtained [a maiden] beautiful in every limb, endowed with virtues, lovely, / who sat as if to enchant the universe, an embodiment of aid to the god whose banner is the sea-monster.

She was a receptacle of play, an embodiment of the accomplishment of joy, endowed with everything, having eyes long as lotus petals, / lotus-faced, with lotus hands, auspicious as a lotus, like a fair image made of gold.
Her radiance was likewise spotless and brilliant; her charms were radiant, and her long locks, / fine and braided, were gracefully curled, smeared with perfumes and decked with flowers.
With hair securely gathered up in firm braids, that young maiden shone with supreme beauty; / and along the parting of her hair a garland of pearls shone like [dewdrops] upon trees.

The auspicious mark at the root of the fair goddess's parting shone like the radiant guru of the Daityas when risen; / on her forehead, O Lotus-born one, it shone with masses of brilliance arising from a lotus of musk.
The radiance of the mark at the root of her parting illuminated the beauty of her form in the world; / in her hair and on her forehead, the pearls continually enhanced her great loveliness.
Just as the gentle moon shines with luster, she too shone with charming movements; / and just as the full moon, cool-rayed, shines with an awning of moonlight,
so her face shone, producing beauty and enchanting the universe; / while the moon indeed has spots and constantly wanes, deprived of its digits,
her face was entirely full, ever joyful, and completely spotless; / beholding her, the lotus found no joy in its own fragrance and blooming.
“This lotus-faced maiden, endowed with all virtues, was fashioned from my own sentiments; / seeing that the wind of the universe blows fragrance from her face, the lotus [shrank].”
Overcome with shame, it at once took refuge in the water and remains there forever. / Wise men of resolute intellect say with thought that she is the treasury of King Love with the arts of the ocean.
She was engaged in playful smiling with teeth like excellent gems, and her face was adorned with lower lips red as bimba fruits.
Fair were her eyebrows, fair her nose; her lovely ears were adorned with gems; / endowed with the luster of gold, her cheeks were full of brilliance.
Three lines shone situated upon her neck, / indeed the three lines of good fortune, virtue, and love right here.
Her breasts were shapely, firm, plump, and round in form, / like two pitchers of Kāma fashioned for his consecration.
Her shoulders shone exceedingly, well-proportioned and endowed with grace; / her arms were lovely, round, smooth, golden, and marked with auspicious signs.
Her lotus hands were well-matched, lotus-hued, very cool, / endowed with divine signs, and marked with lotuses and svastikas.
Her fingers were straight, lotus-like, and furnished with nails; / and her nails were very sharp and gleamed like drops of water.
The complexion arising from her limbs resembled the interior of a lotus; / having the fragrance of a lotus over her entire body, the passionate woman shone like [the goddess] Padmā.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, the daughter of the mountain was exceptionally lovely. / Her two feet resembled red water-lilies, being very smooth and extremely beautiful.
The nails arising on the tips of her feet had the appearance of the lustre of jewels; / and just as is indicated in the scriptures, so too was it seen upon her limbs.
Her limbs adorned with the splendour of all ornaments—necklaces, bracelets, and anklets— / she shone with a girdle upon the hip-string, resounding with tinkling bells.
Clothed in a blue silk garment, the auspicious lady attained supreme splendour, / and endowed with virtues, [she shone] even with an exquisite bodice of brilliant red.
Having obtained supreme prosperity of virtue from the intention formed by Pārvatī, / she derived joy from the wish-granting tree. Then she spoke these words to Śaṅkara:
“Just as was spoken by you, O god, even so has this tree been seen by me. / Whatever kind of intention is formed, just such is seen.”
Sūta said: / Then that fair lady, lovely in all her limbs, approached the side of the two, / and then with devotion she bowed down to the lotus-feet of the two parents of the world.
Then she spoke affectionate, pleasing, and charming words: / “For what reason was I created by you, O lord, O mother? Speak your purpose.”
The blessed goddess said: / “Out of wonder at the tree, a test was indeed made by me in my mind; / and immediately the fruit was obtained, O gentle lady, in the form of your abundant beauty.
By the name Aśokasundarī you will attain renown in the world. / Endowed with all good fortune, you are without doubt my daughter.
Famous in the lunar dynasties as is god Puraṃdara [among gods], / an emperor named Nahuṣa shall become your husband.”
Having thus granted a boon to her, the mountain-born goddess went to the mountain, / to Kailāsa, together with Śaṅkara, filled with supreme joy.

2.103.m: Kuñjala said: / Then Aśokasundarī was born, the foremost of all women; / she took delight in the auspicious Nandana grove, endowed with the qualities of all desires.
With the lovely daughters of the gods, the sweetly smiling woman, / enjoying all pleasures, was skilled in singing and dancing.
The son of Vipracitti, Huṇḍa, fierce and perpetually violent, / roaming at his own will, exceedingly lustful, entered the Nandana grove.
Seeing Aśokasundarī adorned with all ornaments, / at the mere sight of her, the Daitya was pierced by the arrows of Kāma.
He of immense body said to her: “Who are you, and to whom do you belong, O auspicious one? / For what purpose have you come here to this excellent forest?”
Aśokasundarī said: / “Listen now: I am the daughter of Śiva, who is very holy. / I am the sister of Kārttikeya, and my mother is born of the mountain [family].
In childhood innocence, in sport, I have reached the Nandana forest. / But who are you, and why do you question me thus?”
Huṇḍa said: / “I am the son of Vipracitti, endowed with qualities and auspicious marks, / renowned by the name Huṇḍa, arrogant with the pride of strength and valour.
I am the best among Daityas; there is no Rākṣasa equal to me / among gods, in the worlds of mortals, in austerity, fame, or lineage,
or in the other Nāga worlds, in wealth and pleasures, O fair-faced one! / From seeing you, O wide-eyed one, I have been smitten by the arrows of the god of love.
I have indeed come to you for refuge; be gracious, O fair-faced one! / Become my beloved wife, dear to me as my very life.”
Aśokasundarī said: / “Listen, I shall explain the principle of every union. / In this world, there must be a proper match of woman and man of good birth;
similarly, a husband must be one who is equal in virtues to the woman. / This is the way of the world in saṃsāra; listen, O Huṇḍa, according to rule.
Indeed, there is a reason here why I cannot become / your good wife, O king of the Daityas; listen with an attentive mind.
At the time when I was born from the king of trees, O highly intelligent one, / having fully grasped Śambhu’s inclination, I was fashioned by Pārvatī.
With the approval of the god, my husband was indeed designated by the goddess: / in the lunar dynasty there shall be an exceptionally wise, righteous-minded one,
victorious, equal to Indra in valour, like fire in splendour, / all-knowing, true to his word, and equal to Vaiśravaṇa in generosity,
a sacrificer, a master of giving, and like the god of love in beauty; / righteous-minded, named Nahuṣa, a great treasure of virtues and character.
He who was granted to me by the goddess and the god shall be my famous husband. / From him I shall obtain a handsome son endowed with all good qualities,
Yayāti, equal to Indra and Viṣṇu in the world, beloved by the people, / steadfast in battle—him I shall obtain from the grace of Śambhu.
I am devoted to my husband, O hero, and particularly another’s wife. / Therefore, O Huṇḍa, abandon your delusion completely and go away from here.”
Laughing aloud, he spoke these words to Aśokasundarī. / Huṇḍa said: / “What was said by the goddess and the god is not fitting at all.
The righteous-minded one named Nahuṣa will be born in the lunar dynasty; / you are senior in age; a younger man is not suitable.
A younger woman is praised, but a [younger] man is not praised. / When, O gentle lady, will that man become your husband?
Your adolescence and youth will thus go to destruction. / Through the strength of youth, women are always beautiful;
they attain the state of being cherished by men, O fair-complexioned one. / For adolescence is the great treasure of young women, O fair-faced one.
Depending on it, they enjoy pleasures and desires agreeable to the heart. / When will that son of Āyu come, O gentle lady? Listen to me.
Your youth is here this very day, and it will merely go in vain. / Consider: the embryonic state, infancy, and childhood—
when, endowed with youth, will he become suitable for you? / By the power of your youth, drink the wine of springtime!
Enjoy yourself in happiness with me, O wide-eyed one!” / Having heard the words of Huṇḍa, the daughter of Śiva again,
filled with apprehension, spoke to that lord of the Dānavas: / “When the twenty-eighth [age], named the Dvāpara age, arrives, then
the righteous incarnation of Śeṣa, the mighty son of Vasudeva, Bala, / will take the divine daughter of Revata as his wife.
She was born, O illustrious one, in the supreme age called Kṛta; / by the measure of three ages, she is indeed older than Bala.
Revatī became dear to Bala, equal to his very life. / When the future Dvāpara arrives, she will indeed be there.
Long ago, Māyāvatī was born, the excellent daughter of a Gandharva; / having abducted and restrained her, the best of Dānavas, Śambara,
declared that her husband would be the mighty son of Mādhava, / named Pradyumna, the lord of heroes, the son of the lord of the Yādavas.
What is to happen in that future age has been seen by the ancients, / the highly fortunate, wise great souls beginning with Vyāsa.
Even so, O Daitya, are the words seen that were spoken then by the goddess / to me—by the supporter of the universe, the daughter of Himavat.
You, however, greedy with longing and lust, speak of an evil deed / attended by sin, excluded from the Veda and the scriptures.
Whatever is fated for one, firmly, whether auspicious or inauspicious, / according to one's past deeds, that happens to that person.
Whatever well-spoken word comes forth from the mouth of the gods and the brāhmaṇas, / if it comes forth, it is true; it never turns out otherwise.”
By my destiny, indeed, it has been ordained, and also Nahuṣa's: / having considered our union in this way, it was spoken by the Goddess and by Śiva.
Knowing this, find peace; cast away the delusion residing in your mind! / You are certainly not able, O daitya, to shake my resolve.
Devoted to my husband, firm in my mind—who is capable of shaking me? / I will burn you with a great curse! Depart from here, O great asura!”
Having heard those words, the mighty dānava Huṇḍa / pondered in his mind: “How might she become my wife?”
Pondering, the illusory Huṇḍa vanished, / and departing in haste from that place into the sky, / when another day arrived, he created an illusion made of darkness.
Assuming a celestial, illusory form of a woman, that dānava / by illusion took the form of a young maiden, O delighter of my heart.
That maiden, shapely-hipped and assumed through illusion, went then, / endowed with laughing playfulness, to where the daughter of Śiva was staying.
She spoke gently, as it were, to Aśokasundarī: / “Who are you, whose daughter are you, O fortunate one, who stand in the penance grove?
Why, O girl, are you performing this desire-withering penance? / Tell me that, O fortunate one: what is the purpose of this difficult [austerity]?”
Hearing that auspicious speech uttered by the dānava / who was disguised in an illusory form and full of desire, she quickly,
exceedingly distressed, related the full account of her own origin, just as it occurred of old, / and the entire purpose of her penance.
She told also of the assault by that evil-minded dānava; / not knowing the illusory form, she spoke out of friendship.
Huṇḍa said: / “You are devoted to your husband, O goddess, dedicated to righteous vows, / well-behaved, upright in conduct, a great chaste wife!
I too, gentle one, am devoted to my husband, dedicated to devotion to my husband; / for my husband's sake, O fortunate one, do I perform penance, being a great chaste wife.
My husband was slain by that evil-minded Huṇḍa; / for his destruction indeed I perform formidable, great penance.
Come to my sacred hermitage; I dwell on the bank of the Gaṅgā.” / Thus addressed with other charming words that inspired trust,
the daughter of Śiva was bewitched by Huṇḍa in the guise of a female friend; / bewildered by a great delusion, she was drawn along in great haste.
She was brought to his divine, peerless, and very beautiful home, / upon the peak of Meru, O son, the foremost city called Vaiḍūrya,
endowed with every excellence, called Kāñcana, very auspicious, / crowded with lofty palaces, with urns, staves, and flywhisks,
with groves endowed with various trees, dark like rainclouds, / with oblong ponds, wells, lakes, and with rivers and reservoirs,
resplendent with great gems and ramparts adorned with gold, / filled with all desired riches for the dānava.
Aśokasundarī then saw that delightful city / [and said]: “Whose divine abode is this? Tell me, my friend!”
He said: “It belongs to the lord of dānavas whom you saw before; / this is his abode, O highly fortunate one, and I am that foremost of dānavas.
By me you have been brought here by illusion, O fair-complexioned one!” / Having spoken to her, she was led into the exceedingly beautiful golden palace,
furnished with various chambers, resembling the peak of Kailāsa. / Having seated the beautiful woman there upon a swing, afflicted by desire,
the lord of daityas, restored to his own form and tormented by the arrows of desire, / then folded his hands and spoke these words:
“Whatever you desire, gentle one, that very thing I shall grant, without doubt! / Love me, O wide-eyed one, who love you and am tormented by desire!”
The goddess said: / “You, the lord of dānavas, are not able to shake me at all; / even in my mind, no delusion has overtaken me to be entertained!
By great sinners like you, whether gods or lowest of dānavas, / I am unobtainable, without doubt; do not speak again and again!”
She, the younger sister of Skanda, endowed with penance and blazing with great wrath, / desired to destroy that dānava, darting like the tongue of Death.
Again that goddess spoke thus to that lowest of dānavas: / “A terrible deed has been done by you, O wicked one, for the sake of your own destruction!
For the destruction of your own lineage and indeed of your kin, / a blazing flame of fire has been brought by you into your own house.
Just as an ominous bird of prey, arisen with all sorrows, / brings destruction to the house into which it enters,
to all one's kin, together with wealth and family— / when that bird enters a house, it surely desires [its] ruin—
so have I entered your house, seeking your destruction, / and now that of your sons, your wealth and grain, and your lineage.
Your life, lineage, wealth, grain, sons, grandsons, and the rest— / having caused it all to be destroyed by him, I shall depart, there is no doubt.
Just as I was brought away by you while performing supreme penance, / desiring a husband and longing for Nahuṣa, the son of Āyu,
so also shall my husband destroy you, O dānava! / This means having me as its cause was indeed foreseen of old by the God.
True is this worldly saying that wise people sing; / it is visibly seen in the world, yet the foolish do not understand it:
‘By whom, where, and from what cause pleasure, pain, and the like are to be experienced, / that very person experiences it there, from that very cause, without doubt.’
Reap the fruit of your own deed on the earth's surface! / You shall go to the realm of hell from violating another's wife!
Who strikes a very sharp, keen-edged, excellent sword / with the tip of his finger out of anger? Know me to be such now!
Approaching face to face a lion that is enraged and roaring, / who, filled with rash daring, pulls the hairs from its mouth?
I am one of truthful conduct, endowed with self-control, restrained, abiding in penance; / he who desires my ruin, he indeed desires to enjoy me!
He who desires to seize the gem of a living black serpent / is surely one who has been sent by Death!
You, fool, have been sent by Death, deluded by Death; / hence such foolishness has arisen in you; do you not see?
Who indeed, except the son of Āyu, may look upon me? / Any other person surely goes to destruction from gazing upon my form.”
Having thus addressed him, the chaste woman went to the bank of the Gaṅgā, / sorrowful, agitated with grief, restrained and observing vows.
“Previously a terrible penance was performed by me with the desire for a husband; / now, wishing for your destruction, I shall perform dreadful [penance] once again!
When, O wicked one, you are slain by the great-souled Nahuṣa / with sharp arrows resembling thunderbolts and like venomous serpents,
and I see you fallen in battle, sinful, with disheveled hair, covered with blood, / and lifeless, then I shall go to my husband!”
Having made such a firm resolve, the daughter of Śiva / remained steadfast on the unsurpassed bank of the Gaṅgā for the destruction of Huṇḍa.

Like a brilliant, blazing tongue of fire endowed with splendor that would burn the worlds, / glowing with anger, the daughter of the lord of the gods performed difficult penance on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Kuñjala said: / “Having spoken thus, O highly fortunate one, the daughter of Śiva went, / and after bathing in the water of the Gaṅgā, in her city called Kāñcana,
that slender-limbed girl, Aśokasundarī, endowed with truth, / performed penance for the sake of the slaying of Huṇḍa.”
Huṇḍa too became distressed, his mind burned by the curse; / tormented intensely by the fires of her words, he pondered.
Then, summoning his minister named Kampana, he spoke; / he related the whole great occurrence arising from her curse:
“I have been cursed by Aśokasundarī, the virtuous daughter of Śiva: / ‘You shall surely die at the hands of Nahuṣa, my husband!’
Yet that embryo is not even born, and Āyu’s wife is pregnant. / Act in such a way that her curse turns out false rather than true.”
Kampana said: / “Abduct Āyu’s beloved and bring her here; / in this way too, your enemy will not be born.
Or else cause her embryo to miscarry by terrifying means; / in this way too, your enemy will not be born.
Or wait for the time of birth of that wicked Nahuṣa, / and having abducted and brought him here, slay the evil-minded one.”
Thus taking counsel with that Kampana, the Dānava / became prepared for the destruction of Nahuṣa.
Viṣṇu said: / “O noble one, there was a lord of the earth named Āyu, son of Ilā, / a universal monarch, righteous, devoted to the vow of truth,
a king equal to Indra and Upendra in austerity, renown, and strength, / in gifts, highly meritorious sacrifices, truth, and self-restraint.
The best of kings ruled over the earth under a single umbrella, / knowing all righteousness, the ornament of the lunar dynasty.
The king had no son, and because of that he grew grieved; / the righteous-minded one pondered: ‘How can a son be born to me?’
Thus king Āyu fell into anxious thought, / and, concentrating his mind, he made the utmost effort for the sake of a son:
The great ascetic Dattātreya, the great-souled son of Atri, / was sporting with a woman, his eyes red from wine.
Intoxicated with liquor, the righteous one was surrounded by groups of women, / holding on his lap an auspicious young woman, the best of all women.
The brāhmaṇa sang, danced, and drank wine copiously, / devoid of a sacred thread, the supreme lord of great yogins.
With divine flower-garlands, adorned with pearl necklaces, / his body smeared with sandalwood and agallochum, the lord of sages shone resplendent.
Going to his hermitage and seeing that best of twice-borns, the king / made obeisance with his head, bowing down like a rod with deep concentration.
Seeing that best of kings arrived before him with devotion, / the righteous son of Atri then sat in meditation.
In this manner a hundred years passed for that king, O best of men, / his mind unwavering, attaining peace, wholly devoted to worship.
Calling him, [Dattātreya] said this: ‘Why do you trouble yourself, O king? / I am devoid of brāhmaṇa conduct; I possess no brāhmaṇa status whatever.
I crave wine and meat, and I am always attached to a woman. / I have no power to grant boons; attend upon another brāhmaṇa.’
Āyu said: / ‘O noble one, there is no brāhmaṇa superior to you, / the granter of all desires, indeed the supreme lord in the three worlds.
In the lineage of Atri, O noble one, you are the supreme lord Govinda; / in the form of a brāhmaṇa, you indeed are the bird-bannered [Viṣṇu].
Salutations to the God of gods! Salutations to the Supreme Lord! / I have come to you for refuge, O you who are affectionate to those who seek refuge!
Deliver me, O Hṛṣīkeśa! Having assumed an illusion, you remain / as the wise leader of the universe for the creatures residing in the cosmos.
I know you to be the Lord of the Universe, the slayer of Madhu. / Protect me, O Govinda! O you of universal form, salutations to you!’
Kuñjala said: / When much time had passed, Dattātreya said to the best of kings / in the guise of a drunken man: ‘Carry out my word:
Give me wine in a skull-cup, and a cooked meal of meat.’ / Hearing those words, that lord of the earth, Āyu,
eagerly and swiftly brought wine in a skull-cup, / and slicing well-cooked meat with his hand, with haste
the king gave it to Dattātreya, O best of men. / Then the mind of that eminent sage became pleased.
Seeing his devotion, his excellence, and his supreme service to his teacher, / he spoke to that king Āyu, whose mind was bowed in reverence:
‘Choose a boon, may it be well with you, rare on earth, O king! / I will grant you everything, whatever you now desire.’
The king said: / ‘You are a grantor of boons in truth out of compassion, O best of sages. / Give me a son endowed with virtues, all-knowing, gifted with good qualities,
having divine prowess and great splendor, unconquerable by gods and Dānavas, / by kṣatriyas, terrible rākṣasas, Dānavas, and Kinnaras,
devoted to gods and brāhmaṇas, especially a protector of his subjects, / a performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, valiant, affectionate to those seeking refuge,
generous, an enjoyer, noble-minded, learned in the Vedas and Śāstras, / skilled in the science of archery, and devoted to the scriptures,
[He wished for a son] of unimpaired intellect, steadfast, undefeated in battles, / endowed with such virtues, and handsome, from whom the lineage might continue.
Give me a son, O noble one, the upholder of my lineage, / if indeed a boon is to be granted to me out of your grace, O omnipresent one.’
Dattātreya said: / ‘So be it, O noble one! A son shall be born to you / in your house, the founder of your lineage, holy, bringing compassion to all beings,
endowed with these qualities, possessing a portion of Viṣṇu, / a universal monarch, a lord of men equal to Indra.’
Having thus granted the boon, the great yogin indeed gave an incomparable fruit, / and said to the king: ‘Let it be given to your virtuous wife.’
Having spoken thus and dismissed that Āyu bowing before him, / greeting him with blessings, he vanished right there.

2.104.m: Kuñjala said: / When that noble and great sage Dattātreya had departed, / the great king Āyu returned to his own city.
Delighted, he entered the home of Indumatī, endowed with splendor, / abundant in the fulfillment of every wish, resembling the abode of Indra.
That wise king ruled the kingdom just as Purandara does in heaven, / together with Indumatī, the daughter of Svarbhānu, O best of twice-borns.
And Queen Indumatī, by eating the fruit according to Dattātreya’s word, / conceived an embryo endowed with divine splendor.
An incomparable dream was seen by Indumatī, O noble one, / at night, attended by day[like radiance], O father, bestowing great auspiciousness:
Entering inside the house was a man resembling the sun, / a twice-born endowed with a string of pearls, adorned with white garments.
A garland made of white flowers shone upon his neck; / his limbs were beautified with all ornaments, anointed with divine perfume.
He was four-armed, holding a conch in his hand, bearing a mace, discus, and sword, / with a parasol being held over him resembling the disc of the moon,
shining with great majesty, adorned with divine ornaments, / resplendent with a necklace, bracelets, armlets, and anklets,
resplendent with earrings resembling the disc of the moon— / such a highly wise person arrived.
Calling Indumatī, that lovely lady was then bathed with milk / from a conch filled with milk, of the color of the moon.
Filled again and again [with milk], set with gold and jewels; / and a white serpent, handsome, excellent, with a thousand heads,
endowed with a great gem, radiant, an abode full of flames— / it was placed by him near her mouth, and a pearl was given again.
That lord of the gods placed [the pearl] upon the neck of famous Indumatī, / then gave a lotus into her hand and went away to his own abode.
Having seen such a great dream foretelling an excellent son, / the fortunate woman recounted it to Āyu, the lordly ruler of the earth.
Having listened, the great king reflected once more; / then, having summoned his guru, he related the excellent dream
to the most fortunate Śaunaka, omniscient, best among the wise. / The king said: “Tonight, O fortunate one, O best of the twice-born, by my wife
a brahmin was seen entering the house. What is the cause of this dream?” / Śaunaka said: “A boon was granted to you formerly by the wise Dattātreya,
and an auspicious fruit for [obtaining] a son was instructed for kings. / What became of that fruit, O king? To whom was it given by you?”
“It was given by me to my good wife,” thus spoke the king. / Hearing this, the very wise Śaunaka, best among the twice-born, said:
“By the grace of Dattātreya, in your house an excellent son / endowed with a portion of Viṣṇu will be born; there is no doubt.
This which I have told you, O king, is the cause of the dream. / A son equal to Indra and Upendra will be born, of divine valor.
Your son will be entirely devoted to dharma, an increaser of the Lunar dynasty; / he will be accomplished in the science of archery and in the Veda.”
Having spoken thus to the king, Śaunaka went to his home. / Filled with great joy, the king rejoiced with his beloved.

2.105.m: Kuñjala said: / She had gone to the Nandana grove to play with her friends. / There she heard a momentous statement, but one disagreeable to her father,
as celestial bards and noble siddhas spoke with delight: / “In the house of Āyu a son of great valor, whose prowess equals Viṣṇu’s,
an excellent son shall be born, who will make an end of Huṇḍa.” / Hearing such a momentous statement, disagreeable and bringing sorrow,
she returned and reported it before her father. / In brief she related that grief-causing matter
before her father. Having heard it, the father was astonished, / and he remembered the curse formerly made by Aśokasundarī.
For his sake that Aśokasundarī performed austerities. / Solely for the destruction of Indumatī's embryo, that Dānava,
evil and drawn by death, the wicked-minded one made an effort. / Thereupon constantly seeking a flaw in Indumatī,
whenever he saw that queen endowed with beauty, generosity, and virtues, / accompanied by divine splendor and protected by the radiance of Viṣṇu,
endowed with divine splendor, resembling the disc of the sun, / O fortunate one, he constantly stood at her side for [malicious] observation.
From afar that wicked Dānava displayed to her / many sorts of fierce magic, terrifying sights, and dread apparitions.
Endowed with the splendor of the embryo and protected by the radiance of Viṣṇu, / fear never arose in her mind at any time.
The Dānava was frustrated, and his endeavor was fruitless; / the desire of his heart was not realized for the wicked-souled Huṇḍa.
Thus as a full hundred years passed for him watching, / she, the daughter of Svarbhānu, then gave birth to a son.
At night itself her son was born, O best of sons; / with his brilliance he shone exceedingly, like the sun in the sky.
Sūta said: / Then a certain very wicked maidservant came to the lying-in chamber, / practicing impure conduct yet speaking of great auspiciousness.
Knowing everything about her, Huṇḍa, the lowest of Dānavas, / entered the body of that maidservant and thus entered Āyu's palace.
While the multitude of people slept, exceedingly stupefied by slumber, / he abducted that son who resembled an offspring of the gods, and went outside.
Arriving at his own city named Kāñcana, the lowest of Dānavas / summoned his dear wife Vipulā and spoke these words:
“Slay this great sin, my enemy who has assumed an infant's form! / Afterward let him be given into the hand of the cook for food.
Have him cooked without pity in various ways and modes. / Afterward, O fortunate woman, from the cook's hand I shall eat him, no doubt.”
Hearing that speech of her husband, Vipulā was astonished: / “Why has my husband become so pitiless and excessively cruel?
Why and for what reason should he, devoid of forbearance and extremely ruthless, / devour this son endowed with all auspicious marks, resembling the offspring of a god?”
Reflecting thus, filled with compassion, / she again asked her husband: “Why do you devour the child?”
Why are you so enraged and utterly shameless? / Tell me the entire reason in truth, O lord of the Danujas.”
His own fault and the circumstances were briefly reported, / as well as the curse of Aśokasundarī, even by the evil-minded Huṇḍa.
She understood all that reason concerning the Dānava: / 'Indeed this boy must be killed; otherwise my husband will die.'
Having reflected thus, Vipulā, overwhelmed with anger, / summoned the maidservant Mekalā and spoke these words:
'Kill this wicked boy today in the kitchen, Mekalā! / Place him in the hands of the cook so that he may serve as Huṇḍa's food.'
Taking the boy, Mekalā called the cook and said: / 'Carry out the king's command today, and cook this boy!'
When that was heard by the noble cook, / he took the boy from her hand and, raising his knife, was ready.
Indeed, by the splendor of Dattātreya, the god of gods, / the son of Āyu was protected, and he laughed again and again.
Looking upon him laughing, that cook was filled with compassion; / and the chambermaid, filled with compassion, addressed that cook:
'Cook, this infant must not be killed by you thus, O wise one! / Endowed with divine marks, in whose noble family was he born?'
The cook said: / 'You have spoken the truth, gentle lady, words filled with compassion. / Endowed with marks of royalty, beautiful, whose boy is he?
Why should that evil-souled, lowest of Dānavas, Huṇḍa, eat him? / He whose lineage has already been protected by good deeds,
even in distress, in dangerous places, he will live; it cannot be otherwise. / Carried away by the force of the ocean, or having entered the midst of fire,
he lives; of this there is no doubt, he who has karma as his ally. / Therefore, action is performed endowed with dharma and merit.
Men become long-lived through it; from that they proclaim happiness. / Karma is the savior, the protector; it protects and stays awake for one's good.
It constantly brings liberation, bestowing a friendly station. / Action endowed with the merit of gifts, accompanied by pleasant speech,
and joined with benevolence—whoever then performs such good deeds, / him alone does karma protect at all times, without doubt.
Impelled by one's own karma, one has gone to another birth; / what can a father, a mother, or other friends and kinsmen do?
For those struck down by karma, none can be their protectors.' / Sūta said: / 'Indeed, by that very karma, the son of Āyu was protected.
Therefore the cook became compassionate, following the sway of karma; / and the chambermaid likewise became moved by his karma.
By the two of them the son of Āyu, endowed with lovely marks, was protected; / and in the night itself he was carried away from that house to a great hermitage,
to the holy hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, by the chambermaid of virtuous deeds, / right to the auspicious door of a leaf-hut in that great hermitage.
Having left behind that best of boys, she then returned to her own house. / Having slain a deer, the cook indeed prepared its meat.
After feeding the lord of Daityas, Huṇḍa then rejoiced; / the Asura then considered the curse of Aśokasundarī to be null and void.
Filled with immense joy, he, Huṇḍa, was the lord of Dānavas. / Kuñjala said: / 'When the bright dawn arose, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages,
the righteous one, stepped outside the door of the hut and looked. / Seeing a complete child endowed with divine marks,
resembling the full moon, handsome, with lovely eyes, / Vasiṣṭha said: 'Let all the sages come and see the child!
Whose [child is this], and by whom brought at night to the courtyard of my doorway? / Resembling the offspring of gods and Gandharvas, endowed with royal marks,
resembling ten million Kamadevas—behold, O spotless sages!' / Then those best of Brahmins, filled with great curiosity and delight,
beheld the son of the noble Āyu. / That righteous Vasiṣṭha, perceiving the child through spiritual knowledge,
recognized the son of Āyu, along with his character / and the history of that wicked, evil-souled Huṇḍa.
Filled with compassion, that son of Brahmā, the best of Brahmins, / lifted up the sweet child with his hands; and as he took him,
just then the gods made a great shower of flowers upon the child; / the Gandharvas and Kinnaras sang sweet, charming songs;
the sages praised the king's son with Vedic mantras. / Vasiṣṭha, looking upon him, then bestowed a boon upon him:
'Your name shall be famous in the world as Nahuṣa; / you were not agitated [huṣita] even by infantile states, O ruler of men.
Therefore, by the name Nahuṣa, you shall be worshipped by gods!' / The best of Brahmins performed for him the birth rites and the rest,
vows, gifts, renunciations, and the marks of preceptor and disciple. / And having studied the entire Veda, with its six limbs, in the Pada and Krama orders,
and having studied all the scriptures from the best of Brahmins, / the highly intelligent one [learned] the science of archery with its esoteric secrets from Vasiṣṭha,
divine handheld weapons and missile weapons, along with their restraint and release, / the scriptures of knowledge, logic, statecraft, and virtues,
the son of Āyu [learned] from Vasiṣṭha as a devoted disciple. / Thus, endowed with everything, Nahuṣa became exceedingly handsome,
and by the grace of Vasiṣṭha, he became a wielder of the bow and arrow.'

2.106.m: Kuñjala said: / 'The highly fortunate wife of Āyu, the daughter of Svarbhānu, / not seeing that sweet infant, who was godlike and peerless,
lamented loudly, crying out, that woman of fair complexion: / 'By whom was my boy, endowed with marks, of auspicious marks, stolen?
By penance, gifts, sacrifices, and difficult observances / this son was obtained by me, O child, and through terrible hardships!
A son bestowed by the holy, satisfied, noble Dattātreya / has been stolen by whom?' she cried, overcome with grief.
'Alas, son! O child, my dear! Alas, O boy, abode of virtues! / Where are you? By whom have you been taken away? Answer my call!
You are undoubtedly the ornament of the entire Lunar dynasty! / By whom have you been taken away along with my very life-breaths?
Complete with royal and divine auspicious marks, lotus-eyed child! / By whom has the child been stolen today? What shall I do? Where shall I go?
Clearly I know it is the deed done in another birth: / whose deposit was destroyed [by me], that because of that my son was taken?
Or what deceit was committed by me, a sinner, in a previous birth? / For I am undoubtedly experiencing the sorrow of that deed!
Did I become a stealer of jewels, that my jewel of a son was taken / from me by destiny, divine, a mine of incomparable virtues?
Or was a Brahmin doubted [by me], that the fruit of that deed / has been obtained by me without doubt, intensely filled with grief for my son?
Or was hostility against an infant committed by me in another birth? / I am reaping such fruit of the sinful deed!
Or, in the presence of one who was begging during the Vaiśvadeva rite, / was food offered with sacred utterances by Brahmins not given?'
Thus deeply lamenting, the daughter of Svarbhānu, / Indumatī, O highly fortunate one, was agitated with grief and pity.
She fell, fainting from grief, having become utterly distraught, / letting out deep sighs, just like a cow bereft of her calf.
King Āyu, overwhelmed by great grief and sorrow / upon hearing that the child had been abducted, abandoned his fortitude, that king of the earth.
“There is no fruit of austerity, nor is there any fruit of charity, / since my son has been abducted in this manner; therefore it does not exist, there is no doubt.
Dattātreya previously granted me a boon through his favor: / an unconquerable, victorious son endowed with all virtues.
How has an obstacle arisen to that granting of a boon?” / Thus absorbed in anxiety, the sorrowful king wept bitterly.

2.107.m: Kuñjala said: / Then that Nārada arrived from heaven to King Āyu; / having arrived, he spoke: “Why do you grieve, O king?
The abduction of your son today has turned out to be for your welfare, O wise one, / and for that of the gods and others, O great king. Knowing this, do not grieve!
Omniscient, endowed with virtues, possessing all branches of knowledge, / and complete in all arts, your son will return to you.
By him who has abducted today your child resembling a god in qualities, / Death has been brought into his own house, O great king, there is no doubt.
Of him he indeed shall make an end, being of great valor and immense strength. / He will approach you, O king, together with the daughter of Śiva.
Equal to Indra and Upendra, the son will become famous by his own radiance; / he shall also enjoy the status of Indra through his own meritorious deeds.”
Having spoken thus to the king, Āyu, the best of divine sages / departed swiftly before the eyes of the king and his attendants.
When that fortunate Nārada, equal to a god, had departed, / Āyu approached the queen and related all of that.
“The excellent son equal to the best of gods, who was given by Dattātreya, / is truly safe, O queen, by the grace of Viṣṇu.
Having taken the head of him by whom this virtuous son of mine was abducted, / he will return once more, O fair-faced woman.
Nārada said: “O gentle lady, do not grieve at all; / cast off this great delusion which destroys duties and dharma.”
Hearing these words of her husband, Queen Indumatī then / was filled with joy regarding the return of her son.
"What was spoken by the divine ṛṣi, that indeed will come to pass; / a son has been given to me by Dattātreya who is free from old age and death.
It will happen, of this there is no doubt; so it appears to me." / Having reflected thus, she bowed to the eminent twice-born [sage]:
"Obeisance to him, the granter of supreme fulfillment, the great-souled, noble son of Atri, / through whose grace I have obtained a noble son, steadfast, virtuous, and of great merit!"
Having spoken thus, the queen, though deeply grieved, grew calm, / knowing that her son Nahuṣa would indeed return.

2.108.m: Kuñjala said: / The radiant son of Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, best among ascetics, / summoned Nahuṣa and addressed these words to him:
"Go quickly to the forest and bring back abundant forest produce." / Hearing the sage's words, Nahuṣa went to the forest.
There, the mighty Nahuṣa heard an account: / "Here is he, the righteous and valiant one named Nahuṣa,
the highly wise son of Āyu, separated from his mother since infancy; / on account of her separation from him, Āyu's wife weeps bitterly.
Aśokasundarī has performed severe, arduous austerities. / When will that auspicious queen Indumatī behold her son?
He named Nahuṣa, knower of dharma, was stolen away formerly by the Dānavas. / The excellent daughter of Śiva, without any support, has performed austerities.
The maiden Aśokasundarī [has done so] for the sake of Āyu's son. / When indeed will she be united with him?"
Such worldly words spoken by the celestial wanderers, / the righteous Nahuṣa heard, filled with perplexity.
Having collected the forest produce, he went to Vasiṣṭha's hermitage. / Presenting the forest produce to the great-souled Vasiṣṭha,
the righteous one folded his hands in reverence, bowed his neck with devotion, / and addressed the highly wise Vasiṣṭha, best among ascetics:
"Revered lord, listen to an unprecedented utterance spoken by the cāraṇas: / 'Here is Nahuṣa by name, the son of Āyu, separated
from his mother Indumatī with deep sorrow by the Dānavas; / and Śiva's maiden daughter has performed severe austerities
for the sake of this steadfast Nahuṣa,' O spiritual teacher! / All this, spoken by them, was heard by me.
Who is that righteous Āyu, and who is that auspicious Indumatī? / Who is that Aśokasundarī, and who is called Nahuṣa?
This doubt has arisen in me; you ought to dispel it. / Is that Nahuṣa someone else, O highly wise one, and where is he?
Tell me all that, father, along with the underlying cause." / Vasiṣṭha said: "King Āyu is righteous, a mighty sovereign of the seven continents;
his wife is Indumatī, an embodiment of truth and renowned. / The son begotten on her is yourself, an abode of virtues,
begotten by Āyu, the king of kings, an ornament of the lunar dynasty. / The shapely daughter of Hara, adorned with beauty and noble virtues,
named Aśokasundarī, fortunate and sweetly smiling, / has performed austerities in the penance grove without any support for your sake.
You were created by the Creator as her destined husband through union. / Resorting to the bank of the Gaṅgā, she has taken refuge in meditation and yoga.
And the lord of the Dānavas, Huṇḍa, having seen the chaste woman alone, / blazing with ascetic power, fortunate, and lotus-eyed,
endowed with beauty and generous qualities, afflicted by the arrows of desire, / approached her and said: 'Become my wife!'
Hearing his speech, that female ascetic said to him: / 'Do not act rashly, Huṇḍa! Do not prattle again and again!
I cannot be attained by you, hero, especially as another's wife. / By destiny, the mighty son of Āyu was created for me long ago;
the intelligent one named Nahuṣa will become [my husband], of this there is no doubt. / He was granted by a god, full of great splendor. If you act otherwise,
then I will cast a curse by which you will be reduced to ashes.' / Hearing her words, afflicted by the arrows of desire,
he carried her off by deceit and took her to his palace. / Discerning this, O highly fortunate one, that vilest of Dānavas was cursed by her:
'Your death shall happen at the very hand of Nahuṣa!' / Although you were not yet born, she proclaimed it just as it was to happen.
You, the heroic son of Āyu, were seized by that sinful Huṇḍa, / protected by a cook, and sent to my hermitage by a maidservant.
Seeing you in the middle of the forest, the cāraṇas and kinnaras / proclaimed what you heard, O child, and I have now explained it to you.
Slay that evildoer, the vilest of Dānavas named Huṇḍa! / Wipe away the tears she sheds from her eyes!
Go from here, mighty one, and behold the bank of the Gaṅgā; / strike down that lord of the Dānavas and deliver her from the prison house!
Go to Aśokasundarī and become her husband! / All this I have related to you, the reason for your inquiry."
Having spoken thus to Nahuṣa, the highly wise brāhmaṇa fell silent.
Hearing all this wondrous matter uttered by the sage, pondering it within, / wishing alone to put an end to that demon, the son of Āyu then gave way to wrath.

2.109.m: Kuñjala said: / Having bowed down and propitiated Vasiṣṭha, best among ascetics, / and having taken leave, he set out, arrow in hand, bearing a bow.
Venison having been well cooked, the boy was protected through her cleverness and made to eat; / the noble son of Āyu was virtuous, handsome, like a god, and endowed with divine qualities.
With that well-prepared, savory, well-cooked meat endowed with flavor, / the cook, addressing that wicked Daitya, fed him with great joy at that time.
The Dānava consumed the meat rich in delicious flavors; / filled with delight, he went to Aśokasundarī.
His mind clouded by desire, he then said to her swiftly: / "Gentle lady, Āyu's son, your destined husband, has been eaten by me.
Devote yourself to me alone, fair-limbed woman! Enjoy pleasures that fulfill your desires! / What will you do with that mortal whose lifespan has ended?"
Hearing this, the female ascetic, the daughter of Śiva, replied: / "My husband was granted by the gods, free from old age, and devoid of flaw.
His death was not seen even by the great-souled gods." / Hearing her words, the Dānava of wicked conduct
said to that large-eyed woman, laughing again and again: / "Just today the flesh of Āyu's son was eaten [by me], beautiful woman,
of that vile-minded Nahuṣa, a child merely newly born!" / Hearing that statement, she gave way to terrible anger.

Firmly rooted in truth, purified by her austerities, she declared: / "Austerity indeed has been performed by me with my mind and in strict restraint; / by my truth, the son of Āyu shall indeed be long-lived!
Go away from here, vile-behaved one, if you wish to live! / Otherwise, I will curse you once again, of this there is no doubt!"
What was spoken by her was heard by the cook, [who said] to the king: / "O great king, abandon this woman and resort to another!"
Sent away by the cook, that sinful-minded Daitya Huṇḍa / departed in haste toward his own beloved wife.
[The demon] did not know the deed that had been done by the maid and the cook; / everything that had happened was reported to his beloved alone.
Sūta said: / And that Aśokasundarī, indeed, through great ascetic practice, / tormented by sorrow and grief, the ascetic woman had become emaciated.
Thinking of her beloved husband, she meditated on him again and again: / "What do the demons not do by their various means?
Constantly knowing expedients through their wits, constantly through effort as well, / the chiefs of the Danujas always proceed with varied intentions.
Through magical stratagem and union I was abducted by that evil one in the past; / likewise the son of Āyu will surely have been killed.
Having seen whom, by divine decree, there would be my sound lover; / whether by effort one might see him, or whether he is destroyed or not?
Or is that effort superior, or is it the fruit born of that action? / How can destined reality be destroyed, upon which the Veda stands?
How could a special decree made by the gods be otherwise?" / Thus and thus the fortunate woman thought again and again.
There was a Kinnara named Vidvara, born of a great lineage and possessing a huge body; / the upper half of his body from the navel was human, but it was devoid of wings.
two-armed, with a flute in his hand, adorned with a necklace and bracelets, / his limbs anointed with heavenly perfume—arrived together with his wife.
He spoke to her, the joyless daughter of Śaṅkara: / "Why do you worry, goddess? Know that Vidvara has arrived,
me, a Kinnara devoted to Viṣṇu, sent by the best of gods. / You must not feel such sorrow with regard to Nahuṣa.
For the purpose of slaying that wise boy, all deeds were indeed performed / by the evil-acting Huṇḍa, and the son of Āyu was stolen away, O auspicious one.
Yet he was protected by the gods through various means. / Huṇḍa thinks thus: 'The son of Āyu has been carried off by me
and devoured, O wide-eyed lady!'—so he believes, O auspicious one. / Having declared this to you, that lowest of Dānavas departed.
Through the ripening of his own karma and also of his merit, O highly renowned lady, / acquired in a previous birth, that husband of yours lives on.
Those whose lifespan has been fashioned by the very power of merit, / acquired by themselves, O fortunate lady—murderers desire their destruction;
wicked-minded, greatly sinful, defilers of others' splendor, / they devise schemes day after day for the destruction of their renown.
By various means, by poisons, weapons, and so forth, they then / wish to slay that virtuous boy protected by virtuous deeds.
And sinful ones such as Huṇḍa torment him / with stupefaction, immobilization, and so on, with various divisive tactics fouled by violence.
By the application of good deeds acquired in a previous birth, / and also of merit, O fortunate lady, he who possesses merit is well protected.
The stratagems of those sinful ones come to naught, O auspicious one: / devices, rites, mantras, weapons, fire, poisons, and bonds.
They protect the great-souled one who is well guarded by the merits of the gods; / the perpetrators turn to ash, while the possessor of merit stands firm.
The gods are the protectors of that heroic son of Āyu, O auspicious lady, / and all the accumulated merit of austerities, a true treasure.
Therefore the hero Nahuṣa, best among the strong, was preserved / by truth, by that austerity, by merits, and by restraints and disciplines.
Do not suffer dreadful sorrow; cast off groundless grief. / For that righteous one lives in the forest without his mother and father.
He lives alone in an ascetic hermitage, protected by ascetics, / knowing the truth of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, having mastered the science of archery.
Just as the moon shines with its digits through its own luster, / so he too shines with his own accomplishments, O woman of slender waist.
Through sciences, through great merits, through austerities and renown, / the slayer of enemy heroes, destroyer of foes, beloved of the gods, shines forth.
Having slain Huṇḍa, the lord of Daityas, he will obtain you; / together with you as his wife, he will be the sole ruler of the earth,
a great yogi, just as Vāsava is in heaven. / From him, O blessed one, you will obtain a noble son equal to Vāsava,
named Yayāti, knower of dharma, dedicated to protecting his subjects, / and also a hundred daughters endowed with beauty, generosity, and virtues,
through whose merits the great king will go to Indra's world; / Nahuṣa of meritorious valor will enjoy the state of Indra, O goddess.
The righteous one named Yayāti will be your son, / a great king, guardian of his subjects, dedicated to compassion for all living beings.
His sons, however, will be four, endowed with great splendor, / endowed with strength and vigor, master of the science of archery:
The first named Catur, the second named Puru, / the third named Uru, and the fourth, the valiant Yadu.
Such very valiant sons, radiant and exceedingly strong, / will be great-souled, endowed with all brilliance.
And the heroic sons of Yadu will have valor equal to lions; / hear from me now their names as I declare them, auspiciousness to you:
Bhoja, and Bhīmaka, and Andhaka, and Kuñjara, / and he named Vṛṣṇi, very righteous, who will be the support of truth;
the sixth Śrutasena, and Śrutādhāra the seventh, / and the very valiant Kāladaṃṣṭra, mighty, conqueror of time in battle.
The very valiant sons of Yadu are known as the Yādavas, O fair-faced woman; / their sons and grandsons will number in the thousands.
Such will be the lineage of Nahuṣa, O goddess; / completely abandoning sorrow, proceed in happiness.
Your husband of great wisdom will come, O lovely-faced woman; / having slain the Dānava Huṇḍa, he will marry you.
Born of grief, hot tears indeed fall from her eyes; / and he, the bestower of honor, wipes away Indumatī's tears.
Having lifted the sorrow of Āyu, he will deliver his lineage; / having made his father happy, he will become the protector of his subjects.
All this has been told to you, the word of the gods, O auspicious lady; / having abandoned sorrow and grief, dwell in happiness."
Aśokasundarī said: / "When will my husband come, if it has been ordained by the gods? / Speak the truth, O knower of dharma, increase my joy!"
Vidvara said: / "Before long you will see your husband; hear this, O beautiful lady!" / Having spoken thus, the Gandharva went to the abode of the gods.
And that Aśokasundarī performed austerity there, / abandoning desire, anger, and greed, she the daughter of Śiva.

2.110.m: Kuñjala said: / Taking leave of all the sages and Vaśiṣṭha, best of those who practice austerities, / Nahuṣa, eager and desiring to go, set out against the Dānava.
Then all those sages, Vaśiṣṭha and the rest, whose wealth was austerity, / delighted that immensely powerful son of Āyu with blessings.
In the sky, all the gods joyfully beat the kettle-drums; / they cast down a shower of flowers upon Nahuṣa's head.
Then the thousand-eyed god arrived together with the deities / and gave weapons and divine missiles that resembled the sun's splendor.
From the gods the tiger among kings received them, O best of twice-borns; / and with those divine missiles, he resembled a divine form.
Then all those deities said to the thousand-eyed [Indra]: / 'O Lord of gods, let a chariot be given to this Nahuṣa.'
Knowing the opinion of the gods, the vajra-bearer, summoning / his charioteer Mātali, then commanded him, O twice-born one:
'Go to this great-souled one; let him be carried by the chariot, / together with a banner, the very wise son of Āyu prepared for battle.'
And he spoke to the thousand-eyed one: 'I shall execute your command.' / Having spoken thus, he quickly went to the son of Āyu ready for war.
He indeed reported to the king the words of the king of gods: / 'Be victorious in battle, O knower of dharma, with this chariot!
The thousand-eyed one said: “O lord of kings, / slay in battle that evil-minded Dānava Huṇḍa!”
Having heard that, the lord of kings, his hair bristling with joy, [said]: / 'By the grace of the god of gods and of the great-souled Vasiṣṭha,
I shall destroy in battle that evil-minded Dānava, / especially the offender against the gods and my own mother.'
When this great speech had been spoken by the great-souled Nahuṣa, / then the god who bears the conch, discus, and mace arrived in person.
Drawing from his discus a great discus resembling the solar orb, / blazing with burning splendor, with well-rounded spokes and bringing good fortune,
the god gave it indeed to Nahuṣa with great joy. / Śambhu gave him a very sharp trident endowed with fiery energy.
With that excellent trident, he shone as he stood prepared for battle / like a second Śaṅkara, the lord who destroyed Tripura.
Brahmā gave the weapon of Brahmā, Varuṇa the excellent noose, / and a conch resembling the brilliance of the moon, whose sound brought auspiciousness.
Indra gave the vajra and likewise a spear, Vāyu a bow with arrows, / and likewise fire gave the fire-weapon to that great-souled one.
Divine weapons and missiles, many and diverse, / the great-souled gods gave to that king of mighty splendor.
Kuñjala said: / Then the heroic son of Āyu, honored by the gods / and also cheered by the blessings of the sages who know reality,
mounted the divine, radiant chariot, garlanded with gems, / resounding with the sounds of bells, covered with small bells.
On that divine chariot, the joy of the king shone / like the sun on its course in the sky indeed by its own brilliance.
Burning thus by his splendor upon the heads of the Daityas, / he went quickly with speed like Vāyu, who constantly moves,
to where that wicked Dānava stood, accompanied by his forces, / along with that Mātali, the great-souled charioteer.

2.111.m: Kuñjala said: / As that heroic Nahuṣa, equal to the king of gods, went forth to battle, / all the women, eager and accompanied by auspicious songs, gathered around there.
The excellent women of the gods, Rambhā and other apsarases, / and Kinnarīs, longing out of curiosity, sang with melodious voice, O best of men.
Likewise the women of the Gandharvas, endowed with beauty and ornaments, / went there out of curiosity where that king stood.
The city named Mahodaya belonged to that wicked Huṇḍa, / adorned everywhere with divine groves resembling Nandana,
beautified with houses possessing seven courtyards and water-pots, / the excellent city splendid with great flagstaffs bearing banners,
the excellent city resplendent with divine [structures] endowed with all glory, / elevated and reaching the sky, shaped like the peaks of Kailāsa,
with divine forests and groves, and ponds resembling oceans, / full of water, very beautiful, with lotuses and red water-lilies,
and with ramparts made of great jewels, and hundreds of towers, / adorned with moats well-filled with clear waters,
and shining with other great gems, elephants, and horses, / crowded with fair women and men of great radiance,
splendid with various divine wonders—Mahodaya, / that city, the best of kings, the mighty hero Nahuṣa, beheld.
At the edge of the city was a divine forest adorned with divine trees; / the great hero entered it, indeed as an immortal enters Nandana.
Together with the chariot, the righteous-minded one, accompanied by that Mātali— / that lord of kings entered the middle of the forest on the riverbank.
There those divine women, endowed with beauty, arrived; / Gandharva women, knowing the truth of music, sang songs to the best of kings.
And all the bards and panegyrists praised that best of kings, / the king, that son of Āyu, shining like the sun.
Nahuṣa heard the sweet song uttered by the Kinnaras.

2.112.m:
Kuñjala said:
Hearing that very singing sung by the celestial women with fixed melodies,
Śambhu's daughter became agitated there as she reflected.

Rising quickly from her seat, filled with great excitement,
that fair-hipped woman endowed with ascetic disposition went swiftly.

Seeing him, resembling a god, radiant like a divine form,
his limbs smeared with divine scent, adorned with divine garlands,

the prince adorned with divine ornaments and garments,
shining like the sun, endowed with divine marks—

"Could this be a highly wise god, or perhaps a Gandharva?
Or could he be the son of a Nāga, or might he be a Vidyādhara?

I do not see [such a one] among the gods; how could he be born among the Yakṣas?
With such playful charm, even the thousand-eyed [Indra] appears as a hero.

Could this be Śambhu, or could this be the Mind-born [Kāma]?
Or might he be my father's friend, this Paulastya, the lord of wealth [Kubera]?"

While she was reflecting thus, that Rambhā, preeminent in beauty and virtues,
arrived swiftly with her great companions and said to that daughter of Śambhu with a smile:

2.113.m:
Rambhā said:
Abandoning this penance, what are you looking at, auspicious lady?
Indeed, the destruction of penance occurs even from thinking of a man.

Having seen him, O fortunate lady, my mind trembles exceedingly;
I wish to go and make love [with him], having thus become eager.

Such an alteration has arisen in my mind, O fair-complexioned lady;
therefore tell me the cause of it, if there is supreme knowledge in you.

I was created by the noble-minded gods as the wife of Āyu's son;
why then does my mind run eagerly only to make love [with him]?"

Rambhā said:
In all bodily forms, O noble and radiant lady,
resides the Self, Brahman itself, whose nature is eternal knowledge.

Although bound by the senses that aid it, entangled in action,
and bound by the bonds of delusion, it is nevertheless always perfected.

Material nature does not know the art consisting of knowledge and higher realization;
this Self, pure and knowing dharma, knows it, O beautiful woman.

Even anguish of the mind departs upon seeing this high-minded one;
having thus cast away sin, it runs toward truth alone.

He is your husband, the son of Āyu; this is true, there is no doubt.
Upon seeing another man with marks of sin, it would feel apprehension.

Such an ordinance was made by the gods, bound with the bond of truth,
that this son of Āyu will attain the status of her husband.

Thus it was heard by the Self, O auspicious and beautiful lady;
having grasped that true connection of affection, he stands by himself.

It knows no other feeling, but recognizes the son of Āyu;
material nature indeed does not know, O goddess, that her husband has arrived.

Knowing thus, your foremost Self runs toward him this very day;
the Self knows everything; the Self is the eternal deity.

He is that lord of heroes, the mighty one named Nahuṣa;
therefore your mind goes [to him], desiring the true union.

Recognizing him as Āyu's son, O auspicious one, it does not go to another;
all this has been explained to you, eternal and situated in your mind.

Having slain Huṇḍa, the most terrifying and vile Dānava, in battle,
he will lead you to his own abode, the excellent house of Āyu.

The lord of heroes was abducted by the Daitya, but spared by his own merit;
from his childhood, the lord of heroes was separated from his kin.

Bereft of father and mother, he grew up in the great forest;
he will certainly go to his father's house along with you now."

Hearing this speech of Rambhā, the daughter of Śiva,
filled with great joy, said to the ocean-born [Rambhā]:

"He alone is that true Self, my most mighty husband;
my mind runs exceedingly [toward him], which was distressed and agitated by sorrow.

There is no deity equal to the mind; it knows with absolute certainty;
this truth has been perceived by me, most wonderful, O sweet-smiling one!

Even seeing a man endowed with divine marks resembling Kāma,
my noble heart did not run toward him as it does toward him, O friend.

In that manner it does not run [toward another], O auspicious lady; it acknowledges no other man.
Both of us together with the companions must certainly go to his home."

Having spoken thus, Rambhā set out to go;
knowing her eager to go near Nahuṣa,

Rambhā then said to her: "Why, O goddess, are you not going?"
Sūta said:
Together with her friend Rambhā, [approaching] Nahuṣa endowed with heroic marks,

having come very close to him, she sent that friend [saying]:
"Go to this noble Nahuṣa of divine form,

tell this tale: 'For your sake she has arrived.'"
Rambhā said:
"So shall I do, O friend, what is most pleasing to you, O lady of good vows."

Having spoken thus, Rambhā went to Nahuṣa, the prince,
the hero holding bow and arrows, like a second Indra.

Rambhā, having gone, delivered the excellent words of her friend:
"O noble son of Āyu, I, Rambhā, have approached you.

I have been sent, O hero, by that daughter of Śiva.
For your sake, formerly, by the god of gods and by the goddess,

an excellent, best form of a wife was created, rare in the worlds,
difficult to be attained by the best of men, gods, Indras, ascetics,

Gandharvas, Pannagas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas of meritorious marks;
she herself has come for your sake; listen now!

She is a jewel among women, O highly wise one, full [of virtues], formed by merit,
named Aśokasundarī, who stood in penance for your sake.

She performed extreme penance, and desires you always;
knowing this, O noble one, accept her who is devoted to you.

Except for you, that fair-hipped woman does not seek any man."
Nahuṣa, having heard and grasped the words spoken by her,

then gave an answer: "O Rambhā, let my words be heard!
I know all that which has been spoken by you before me.

It was told before me previously by the noble Vasiṣṭha;
I know everything about this supreme penance of hers.

Hear the reason, O auspicious one, by which happiness will come about:
without slaying the Dānava Huṇḍa, I will not go to the excellent woman.

I know all this event very well just as it is,
that your birth was for my sake, and that penance was performed by you.

You were made my wife by destiny, of this there is no doubt;
having resolved for my sake, penance was performed by you.

Therefore, you, observing vows, were abducted by that very wicked one;
and from the lying-in chamber, by that vile Dānava,

while still a child, O goddess, I was separated from my father and mother.
Therefore, I shall surely slay that vile Dānava Huṇḍa.

Afterwards, I will lead you to Vasiṣṭha's hermitage.
Thus tell my beloved woman, Rambhā; may good betide you."

Thus dismissed by him, she went back quickly,
and told the goddess Aśokasundarī [the words] of his.
In brief, all that [was related] by that Rambhā, O best of the twice-born; / and having understood that good speech, that Aśokasundarī,
endowed with joy on account of the very heroic Nahuṣa, / remained there with her, her good friend Rambhā, at that time,
[thinking,] 'Let me indeed constantly watch what kind of valor my husband has.'

2.114.m: Kuñjala said: / Then all those Dānavas, the attendants of Huṇḍa, / just as they had heard the conversation of Nahuṣa with Rambhā,
reported all the well-spoken words to Huṇḍa, the lord of Daityas. / Having heard it, he became enraged, and then spoke words to a messenger:
'Go, hero, by my command, and ascertain about that man! / A man is conversing with her, with the daughter of Śiva.'
Having heard his master's command, the Dānava quickly went; / in a secluded spot, he spoke this word to the hero Nahuṣa,
who stood with a divine chariot, horses, and charioteer, / terrifying indeed in the assembly with his bow and divine arrows:
'Whose man are you? For what purpose, or by whom have you been sent? / By this Rambhā, and today by another, the daughter of Śiva,
what was said? Tell all that clearly before me! / How is it that you do not fear Huṇḍa, the crusher of the gods?
Tell me all this, if you wish to live! / Go quickly, do not stay; the lord of Dānavas is hard to withstand.'
Nahuṣa said: / 'That powerful King Āyu, who is the ruler and lord of the seven continents— / know me to be his son, the destroyer of all Daityas,
celebrated by the name Nahuṣa, a worshiper of gods and brāhmaṇas, / abducted in infancy, O Dānava, by your master Huṇḍa.
This daughter of Śiva was also abducted of old by that Daitya; / she performs severe penance, and [it is] for the slaying of Huṇḍa.
I who was taken as an infant at first by you from the lying-in chamber, / and given into the hand of a maidservant, and also of a cook by that wicked one
for the purpose of slaying—listen, O sinner—that very person am I, who have come today! / Both of this Daitya Huṇḍa, wicked and evil-doing,
and of the other terrible Dānavas, I shall dispatch [them] to the abode of Yama! / Know me thus, O most sinful one!' Thus speak to the Dānava!
Having heard all that from the great-souled Nahuṣa, / that evil-minded one went to Huṇḍa and related his words.
Hearing it from his mouth, the lord of the Diti's sons quickly grew furious: / “Why was he not slain by that wicked cook and that maidservant?
Like an ignored disease, he has grown strong. / Now I will slay him along with that daughter of Śiva,
that vile son of Āyu in battle, with these stone-sharpened arrows!” / Having thought thus, he spoke these words to his charioteer:
“Yoke the chariot with excellent, auspicious horses!” / Calling the army commander, agitated, he said:
“Let my army be prepared! Arrange valiant elephants, / horses with their riders, warriors with banners, parasols, and chowries.
Mobilize my fourfold army at once without delay!” / Having heard that, the army commander of Huṇḍa,
being very wise, quickly made all arrangements according to rule. / Surrounded by that great fourfold army,
he marched against the heroic Nahuṣa, who bore bow and arrow in battle, / who was mounted on Indra's chariot, the foremost of all who bear weapons,
rising in battle, a hero hard to be reached by gods and Dānavas. / The gods of great splendor, standing in their aerial chariots in the sky, looked on at him
blazing with flames of radiance like a second sun. / Sūta said: Then all those Dānavas showered him with the best of arrows,
with swords, nooses, great pikes, javelins, and axes. / They fought in battle with that great-souled Nahuṣa,
raging and roaring, just like clouds upon a mountain. / Observing their prowess, the glorious son of Āyu,
having strung his bow, which was equal to Indra's weapon, twanged it so that it sounded. / The sound of the bow of that great-souled one was like a thunderclap,
produced by Nahuṣa, striking terror into the Dānavas, O brāhmaṇas. / At that mighty noise, the Dānavas trembled,
their hearts overcome with stupor, their courage broken in the great battle.

2.115.m: Kuñjala said: / Then that radiant, great-souled one, bearing his bow and standing ready, / just like wrathful Time wishing to destroy the worlds, so wished to destroy the Dānavas.
With arrays of great weapons, resembling the radiance of the sun and exceedingly brilliant, he struck down the Dānavas; / just as the wind here uproots trees, so the king struck down the Dānavas.
Just as the wind, by its own force and energy, scatters a celestial mass of clouds, / so that king destroyed the proud asuras with his sharpest, excellent arrows.
None of the Dānavas could endure the shower of arrows from that great-souled one; / some died, some fled, and some perished from the great battlefield.
Sūta said: / Seeing that son of the king, possessor of great splendor, deeply wise, and destroyer of great Dānavas, / the evil-minded Huṇḍa became furious.
Going forward and standing firm, he called out in battle: “Stand, stand! / Today, son of Āyu, I will send you to the presence of Yama!”
Nahuṣa said: / “Here I stand in battle! Behold, I have come to slay you! / I shall indeed kill you, a Dānava of wicked intent!”
Having spoken thus, taking up his bow and arrows resembling tongues of fire, / he shone in the battle beneath the parasol held over him.
He spoke these words to Mātali, the divine charioteer of Indra: / “Drive my chariot today straight toward Huṇḍa.”
Thus addressed by that hero, Mātali of swift valor / urged on the horses, which were as swift as a mighty wind.
Then the steeds flew up like swans into the sky, / with his moon-colored parasol and the chariot bearing flags.
Just as the sun shines when it reaches the vault of heaven, / so did the son of Āyu shine in battle with his splendor and prowess.
Then Huṇḍa, mounted on his chariot, radiant with his own splendor, / equipped with all weapons, likewise stood steadfast in the vow of a hero.
The battle between the two heroes caused astonishment to the gods; / then, O very wise one, it became dreadful and terrifying.
With sharp, pointed, heron-feathered arrows, / Huṇḍa struck the king in the chest between his arms.
Then, pierced on his forehead with five arrows, he grew enraged; / and pierced with those arrows, the king shone all the more,
like the sun rising red with wreaths of rays; / his limbs smeared with blood, and with the golden arrows fixed in his body,
the king shone like the morning sun in the sky. / Seeing his prowess, he spoke these words to the Dānava:
“Wait, wait a moment, Daitya, and behold my swiftness!” / Having said this in the fight, he struck the Daitya with ten arrows.
Struck by him on the face and forehead, the very mighty one swooned and fell down. / As the celestial gods above looked on,
a joyous shout was raised by the gods, cāraṇas, and siddhas: / “Victory, victory, O king of kings!” and they blew their conches again and again.
That tumultuous roar raised by the deities / entered the ear-cavity of the swooning Huṇḍa.
Hearing it, he took up his bow and an arrow like a venomous serpent: / “Stand, stand in battle! I am not dead from your strike!”
Having spoken thus, rising up again with agility, / he struck Nahuṣa once more with twenty-one arrows.
with one in the hand's grip, with four in the arms, / with four his great horses, and with one indeed his parasol;
having pierced Mātali with five, the chariot box with seven, / the Dānava struck the flagpole with three sharp, peacock-feathered arrows.
Beholding the taking up, aiming, target-hitting, and releasing of that evil-souled one, / and his swiftness, the deities were astonished.
Seeing that prowess of his, the king said to the foremost of Dānavas: / “You are heroic, well-trained, resolute, and skilled in battle!”
Having spoken thus to that Dānava, the king, drawing his bow / with swift prowess, pierced him with ten arrows.
With three he cut down his flag, which fell to the earth; / with four arrows he felled his horses;
with one, swift in prowess, he severed his parasol; / with ten, his charioteer was dispatched to the abode of Yama;
severing his armor with ten arrows, it was shattered to pieces; / and on all his limbs he pierced the lord of the Danu's sons with thirty arrows.
With his horses slain, deprived of his chariot, holding arrows in hand and bearing his bow, / he rushed forward violently, showering sharp arrows.
Bearing sword and shield, the Daitya rushed at the king; / as Huṇḍa came running, the king cut off his sword;
with sharp crescent-tipped arrows, the king shattered his shield. / Then that evil-minded Huṇḍa, looking around on every side,
swiftly seized a club and hurled it with quick prowess; / the king then saw it approaching with the speed of a thunderbolt.
Then, by his prowess, with ten sharp, crescent-headed arrows, / he brought down that roaring club from the sky.
