Seeing his club fallen onto the earth in ten pieces, / lifting his mace with speed, he rushed against the king.
With his sharp-edged sword, he severed his arm; / it fell to the earth along with the mace, adorned with armlet and bracelet.
Then, having let out a great roar like the crash of a thunderbolt, / his limbs smeared with blood, running in the great battle,
seized by intense fury, he wished to swallow the king; / unstoppable, he came close to the king's side.
Struck in the chest by Nahuṣa with a great lance, / the Dānava suddenly fell to the earth like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
When that Daitya fell to the earth, the other Dānavas fled; / some entered into strongholds, and some took refuge in Pātāla.
The gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas attained great delight, / when that great sinner was slain by high-souled Nahuṣa.

When that best of Daityas was slain in the great battle, all the gods attained joy; / and having regained that maiden endowed with divine beauty, enhanced by austerities, the son of Āyu was overjoyed.

2.116.m: Kuñjala said: / Joyful along with Rambhā, the virtuous, ascetic girl Aśokasundarī, / having obtained the valiant Nahuṣa, spoke to him:
"I am your wife according to dharma, ordained by the gods, a woman who practices tapas; / marry me, O hero, if you desire dharma in this world.
Constantly thinking of you, I have remained in austerity; / by the grace of dharma, O best of kings, you have been obtained by me."
Nahuṣa said: / "O gentle lady, since for my sake you have remained steadfast in tapas, / by the guru's word I will become your husband in an auspicious hour.
Let the two of us go together with this Rambhā, O lovely lady." / Having seated that girl and the charming Rambhā in the chariot,
with that very excellent chariot, toward Vasiṣṭha's hermitage / the highly renowned one went with great speed together with the two of them.
Seeing that brahmin who had arrived at the hermitage and bowing down, / along with her, the one of great splendor was filled with immense joy.
How the fight occurred in battle, and how the vile Dānava was slain— / he reported everything to high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
Vasiṣṭha too, having heard of Nahuṣa's exploit, / filled with great joy, congratulated him with blessings.
When an auspicious lunar day and planetary ascendant arrived, the best of sages / performed their marriage in the presence of fire and brahmins.
Having thus congratulated the couple with blessings, they were sent off again: / "Go quickly and see your mother and father, O highly wise one!
Indeed, having seen you, O virtuous one, may your mother and father / swell with joy, just like the ocean at the full moon."
Thus dismissed by the sage, the son of Brahmā, / the hero, swift in prowess, departed in that very excellent chariot.
Having bowed to that lord of the twice-born, he then went with Mātali / to his own city to see his father and likewise his mother.
Sūta said: / Then an apsaras named Menakā was sent by the gods; / for the wife of Āyu had fallen into an ocean of grief through intense sorrow.
She spoke to the highly fortunate queen Indumatī: / "Cast aside your grief, O highly fortunate one! Behold your son along with your daughter-in-law!
Having slain the sinful Dānava who abducted your son, / he is arriving with his wife, endowed with heroic splendor."
Menakā narrated to Indumatī the noble conduct / that had been performed by Nahuṣa in that battle.
Having heard the words of Menakā, filled with great joy, / she spoke with a choked voice, 'O friend, do you speak the truth?
What you have spoken is nectar-like, very pleasing, and heart-cheering; / life itself, my very all, should indeed be given by me to you.'"
Having thus addressed her, the queen said this to the king: / "Your mighty-armed son has indeed arrived now!
And this best of apsarases is telling me, O great king!" / Having thus addressed her husband, she paused, overjoyed.
Hearing this, the lord of kings spoke to his beloved: / "Formerly it was indeed said by the sage Nārada, O highly fortunate one:
'Grief for your son must never be felt by you, O king; / having slain that Dānava by his great valor, the son will return.'
Indeed, what was spoken formerly by the sage has come to pass as true; / how could his word ever be otherwise, O queen?
Dattātreya, the best of sages, the visibly manifest god, / was formerly served by you, O queen, and by me with austerities.
By him a jewel of a son, bearing a portion of Viṣṇu, was granted, / who will forever slay the enemy, the sinful-minded Dānava,
the slayer of all Daityas, the protector of subjects, possessing great strength; / this excellent son, a portion of Viṣṇu, was given to me by Dattātreya."
Having thus spoken to Queen Indumatī, the king then / arranged a great festival for the arrival of his son.
Filled with great joy, he again remembered Viṣṇu,

who is completely perfect, surrounded by hosts of gods, the embodiment of bliss, the one supreme truth, / the remover of afflictions, the bestower of happiness upon mortals, and the giver of supreme liberation here to true Vaiṣṇavas.

2.117.m: Kuñjala said: / Nahuṣa, along with his beloved and with Rambhā, / also with the heavenly and excellent chariot of Indra,
reached the city named after an elephant, endowed with all splendors, / accompanied by divine auspicious marks and adorned with palaces,
furnished with golden archways, decorated with banners, / and graced with bards and Cāraṇas amidst the sounds of various instruments,
adorned by virtuous men resembling divine forms, / by women of celestial beauty, by elephants, horses, and chariots,
crowded with various auspicious sounds and the chanting of the Vedas, / and then with the sounds of songs, instruments, lutes, and flutes.
Filled with every beauty, he entered that best of cities; / and he was honored by brahmins with auspicious Vedic chants.
The hero saw his father and his mother of great virtue; / filled with great joy, he bowed to his father's feet.
Aśokasundarī, she of lovely face, / bowed again and again to the feet of them both with devotional disposition.
And Rambhā bowed too and showed her affection. / Having greeted and conversed with his guru, the prince
asked his mother and father after their good health. / Thus addressed, the highly fortunate one, experiencing goosebumps of joy,
Āyu said: / "Today itself all afflictions have vanished, and both grief and sorrow are gone! / By seeing you, O son, the world rejoices with great satisfaction.
I have become one whose purpose is accomplished, now that you, endowed with great luster, are born; / having brought about the deliverance of your own lineage, I myself have been delivered!"
Indumatī said: / Just as the great ocean rises on the full moon upon seeing the splendor of the moon, / so do I, O fortunate one, at the sight of you.
I am exalted, I am delighted, I am overwhelmed with joy! / At your sight, O very wise one, O bestower of honor, I have become blessed.
Having thus spoken to that son, embracing that best of sons / and also smelling his head, just as a cow [smells] her own calf,
welcoming the recovered son, Nahuṣa of godlike form, / the virtuous queen Indumatī then honored him with blessings.
Sūta said: / Then that son told his virtuous mother, Queen Indumatī, / the narrative of his own abduction,
as well as the birth and obtaining of his wife, O greatly renowned one, / and how the battle with Huṇḍa took place, and also the slaying of Huṇḍa.
All that which had happened was indeed recounted by him in brief / to both his parents, bringing joy to the two of them.
Having heard their son’s heroic exertion, the parents, / filled with great delight, became fulfilled in heart.
Nahuṣa, taking his bow, upon Indra’s chariot indeed, / conquered the entire earth with its seven continents and cities.
He surrendered the earth, filled with wealth, to his father, / continually gladdening his father with righteous deeds of giving and noble actions.
Then he caused his father to sacrifice with the Rājasūya and other sacrifices, / with great sacrifices and gifts, and with vows, observances, and self-restraint.
With abundant gifts, through renown, and with virtuous sacrifices yielding great prosperity, / those two parents were made completely fulfilled by Āyu’s son.
Then the gods, having assembled at the supreme city called Nāgāhvaya, / consecrated the great-souled Nahuṣa, the crusher of heroes.
Having consecrated him in his own kingdom along with Śiva’s daughter [Aśokasundarī], / by the sages, the great Siddhas, and that king Āyu,
King Āyu, righteous-minded and of great renown, together with his wife in his own body, / went to heaven, duly honored by the gods and Siddhas.
Leaving Indra’s realm, he went to the world of Brahmā; then, / honored by the gods along with the sages, he went to the world of Hara [Śiva].
Through his own deeds and through the splendid power of his son, / that king, through his merits, went to the world of Hari and dwells there.
By men renowned for virtuous deeds, such supreme merit / should be brought forth, O fortunate one; what use are other [sons] who cause sorrow?
Just as the righteous Nahuṣa was born, the deliverer of his father, / the sustainer of his entire lineage, Nahuṣa, learned in wisdom.
All this deed of that king has been told to you. / What else shall I declare to you? Speak, my son Kapiñjala.
A mortal who hears this auspicious and pure deed, endowed with renown, / of Āyu’s son, having enjoyed pleasures, goes to the abode of Murāri.

2.118.m: Kapiñjala said: / Formerly, dear father, at the mouth of the Gaṅgā, an excellent woman was weeping, / and drops of tears were falling from her two eyes into the great water.
Plunging into the middle of the Gaṅgā, they became lotuses, / flowers of divine appearance, fragrant and large.
Why, dear father, do pure drops of tears fall from her lovely eyes / into the water of the Gaṅgā, O fortunate one?
And an ascetic reduced to bones and skin, wearing matted hair and bark garments, / gathers those fragrant lotuses;
bringing those divine flowers of golden color, he worships Śiva. / Tell me, who is that woman, or who is he, O very wise one?
Having worshipped Śiva, why does he subsequently lament? / Tell me all this, if I am dear to you.
Kuñjala said: / Listen, my child, I shall tell you the divinely ordained story, / a narrative that destroys all sins, and also of the great-souled Viṣṇu.
That very powerful Huṇḍa who was slain in battle by Nahuṣa— / his son, the famous Vihuṇḍa, undertook asceticism.
Having heard that his father, together with his ministers and retinue, was slain / by Nahuṣa, the heroic and mighty son of Āyu,
he performed asceticism out of rage, striving to slay the gods. / And the prowess of that wicked one, magnified by asceticism,
all the gods knew to be irresistible on the field of battle. / That son of Huṇḍa, Vihuṇḍa, set out to destroy the three worlds.
"I will avenge my father's enmity; I will slay the mortals and the gods!" / Thus resolved that evil one, a thorn to gods and brāhmaṇas.
He began creating turmoil and tormented the subjects; / burned by his very splendor, the gods, with Indra at their head,
sought refuge with the God of gods, the great-souled Viṣṇu, / the God of gods, Lord of the universe, holding the conch, discus, and mace.
And they said, "Protect us always from the great fear of Vihuṇḍa!" / The glorious Viṣṇu said: / "May all the deities prosper in great comfort, O great lords!
I shall destroy Vihuṇḍa, the most wicked thorn to the gods." / Having thus addressed those gods, Janārdana, employing illusion,
Himself of great renown, stayed there in the Nandana grove; / then He assumed the illusory form of a woman endowed with virtues.
Viṣṇu's glorious illusion, bewildering the entire universe, / assumed an incomparable form—the bewitching illusion of Viṣṇu—
endowed with beauty and grace, for the sake of slaying Vihuṇḍa. / Kuñjala said: / He went to the celestial path to slay the gods.
Then, at the edge of the Nandana grove, the lord of the Daityas saw the illusory form. / Bewildered by her, the Daitya was pierced by the arrows of desire.
He did not recognize that excellent woman to be Death incarnate, bringing about his own destruction. / Seeing her shining like fresh gold, endowed with the wealth of beauty,
the sinful Vihuṇḍa, inflamed with lust, spoke to that excellent woman: / "Who are you, and to whom do you belong, O woman of lovely hips, agitator of my mind?
Grant me union, O auspicious one! Protect, protect me, O fair-faced woman! / In exchange for union with you, O goddess, whatever you now desire,
all that I shall give, O fortunate one, even what is difficult for gods and Dānavas to obtain!" / The illusory woman said: / "If you wish to enjoy me, give me my bridal portion, O Dānava!
Worship Śaṅkara with seven crore flowers / born of Kāmodā, divine, fragrant, and difficult for the gods to obtain.
Place a garland made of those flowers around my neck, O Dānava! / O fortunate one, give me this bridal portion;
then I will become your beloved wife, there is no doubt." / Vihuṇḍa said: / "O goddess, I will do so; I grant the boon you have requested."
The lord of the Daityas wandered through all the sacred, divine forests, / afflicted by desire, but did not see that tree.
Wherever he went himself, he inquired about the [tree] called Kāmodaka. / "There is no tree named Kāmodaka," so the people told him.
Inquiring thus, that wicked one, afflicted by the arrows of desire, / went to Bhārgava [Śukra] and asked, bowing his neck in devotion:
"Tell me of the lovely Kāmodaka tree endowed with flowers." / Śukra said: / "Kāmodā is not a tree; it is a woman, O Dānava.
Whenever she laughs, delighted during conversation, / from that laughter, O Daitya, fragrant and excellent [flowers] are born.
"These are divine flowers, [born] of Kāmodā, without a doubt: / lovely, yellow flowers endowed with fragrance.
Even with one such flower, whoever worships Śaṅkara— / Śaṅkara fulfills his desired great wish.
From her weeping, O Daitya, there arise, without doubt, / flowers of that very kind, red and large.
Lacking fragrance, O Daitya, one must not touch them." / Thus was the word spoken by Śukra heard by him.
He said, "Where is that Kāmodā, O son of Bhṛgu?" / Śukra said, "At Gaṅgādvāra, supremely holy, destroying great sins,
a city named Kāmoda was built there by Viśvakarman. / In the city of Kāmoda, a woman adorned with divine delights,
and resplendent with ornaments, is well worshipped by all the gods. / You must go right there; that excellent Apsaras is to be honored.
By some holy means, O Dānava, make her laugh!" / Having spoken thus to the Dānava, the king of yogins,
that Śukra of great splendor, ceased, and set out for his own business.

2.119.m: Kapiñjala said: / "O father, from whose laughter indeed arise such lovely / divine-smelling flowers, difficult to attain by gods and asuras,
why do all the deities desire them, O highly intelligent one? / Śaṅkara finds delight when well worshipped with laughter-flowers.
What is the virtue of that flower? Tell me that at length! / Who might that Kāmodā be? Whose daughter is that excellent woman?
And from her laughter, O fortunate one, good flowers arise. / What is the virtue? Tell that whole story at length."
Kuñjala said: / "Formerly, the gods together with the great Daityas, having forged an excellent friendship, / actively churned the ocean of milk for the sake of the nectar.
From the churning of the gods and Daityas, a set of four gem-like maidens / was revealed first by Varuṇa, and then likewise by Soma.
Afterward, the sacred nectar placed in a pot was revealed. / The set of four maidens originally wished for the welfare of the gods:
one named Sulakṣmī, and the second was Vāruṇī; / one was known as Jyeṣṭhā, and they declare another as Kāmodā.
Among them, the best and most excellent was born first, O wise one; / therefore she is renowned as Jyeṣṭhā, always worthy of worship in the world.
Vāruṇī took the form of drink and was born from the foam of the milk; / and from the wave of the nectar, she named Kāmodā arose.
King Soma and Lakṣmī were both born from the nectar as well. / Soma, the ornament of the three worlds, became dear to Śaṅkara.
Vāruṇī was born for the gods as a destroyer of death and disease; / Jyeṣṭhā was born bestowing great merit upon those desiring the world's welfare.
The goddess arisen from the nectar, named Kāmodā, bestowing merit, / will, for the delight of Viṣṇu, assume the form of a tree.
She will always bring delight to Viṣṇu; / she will surely become holy, named Tulasī, without a doubt.
With her, the Lord of the Universe will sport, without a doubt. / Whoever, taking a single leaf of Tulasī, offers it to Kṛṣṇa—
he wonders at his favors: 'What shall I give to him?' / Thus he would always think; he becomes pleasing to him.
Thus that ocean-born one was formerly named Kāmodā. / When that goddess laughs, speaking with faltering joy,
lovely, fragrant, unfading fine flowers / indeed fall from her mouth. Whoever, taking pains, gathers them,
and worships the god Śaṅkara, Brahmā, and Mādhava, / the gods are pleased with him and give whatever he desires.
And when she weeps, afflicted by some sorrow, / from the tears of her eyes they indeed arise and fall.
And they too, O fortunate one, are lovely and very large; / but whoever worships Śaṅkara with those lacking fragrance—
to him sorrow and torment arise; of this there is no doubt. / If a wicked-minded one worships the gods even once with such flowers,
the gods cause him sorrow in that case, without a doubt. / All this excellent story of Kāmodā has been told to you.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having reflected and seen the valor and recklessness, / the effort and rashness of that sinful Vihuṇḍa,
sent Nārada, [saying,] 'Delude this unapproachable one!' / Then Nārada, having heard the words of the great-souled Viṣṇu,
went up to the Daitya chief, the wicked Dānava who was going toward Kāmodā, / and as if smiling, said to him:
"Where are you going, O Daitya king, quickly and so anxious? / By what task, for whose sake, and impelled by whom are you now [going]?"
Bowing to the son of Brahmā with folded hands, he replied: / "I have set out for the Kāmoda flowers, O best of the twice-born!
That righteous one said to him: "What is your purpose with the flowers?" / Again he told the foremost of Brahmins the reason for his enterprise:
"In a region of the Nandana forest, there is a certain fair-faced woman; / by the mere sight of her, I have fallen under the power of passion.
By her I was told, O chief of Brahmins: 'With flowers produced from Kāmodā, / worship Mahādeva with seventy million flowers!
Then I shall become your dearly beloved wife, without a doubt.' / For that purpose I have set out today toward the city named Kāmoda.
I will make love to her, the ocean-born one; listen now! / With delightful thoughts and loud laughs I will make her laugh repeatedly.
Being delighted, that fortunate one will laugh again and again; / that faltering laugh, O Brahmin, will further my purpose.
From that laughter, divine blossoms will fall; / with them, now, I will worship the god, the beloved of Umā.
Satisfied by the offering of that worship, he will grant me the fruit— / the Lord, the master of all beings, Śaṅkara, the creator of the world."
Nārada said: / "You should not go there, O Daitya, to that supreme city named Kāmoda! / Viṣṇu is there, highly intelligent, the bringer of destruction to all Daityas.
By which means the flowers named Kāmoda / will come into your hands, O Dānava, that means I shall tell you.
They will fall into the waters of the Gaṅgā, without a doubt; / carried along by the divine waters, they will arrive right now.
Receive them—lovely and very large! / Having collected those flowers, accomplish your heart's desire."
Nārada, having thus deluded the foremost Dānava, then / that righteous-minded one reflected once again:
"How might she shed tears? By what means could she become grieved?" / While that Nārada was thus thinking for a moment,
then an idea occurred [to him], and he went to the city named Kāmoda.
